title: Algebraic extension gives torsion quotient of value groups, in element form
statement: Let $K\subseteq E$ be fields and suppose every element of $E$ is algebraic over $K$ [def-pc-field-extension] [def-weil-algebraic-element]. Let $V\subseteq E$ be a subring such that for every $z\in E^\times$ either $z$ or $z^{-1}$ lies in $V$. For every $x\in E^\times$ there exist an integer $n\geq1$, an element $a\in K^\times$, and an element $u\in E$ with $u,u^{-1}\in V$, such that $x^n=au$. Thus every class in $E^\times/V^\times$ has a positive multiple in the image of $K^\times$, where $V^\times=\{u\in E^\times:u,u^{-1}\in V\}$.

proof.text: Put $U=\{v\in V:v\ne0,\ v^{-1}\in V\}$ and $M=V\setminus U$. Thus $U$ is precisely the set of units of $V$: an inverse in the subring is the field inverse. If $r\in M$ and $b\in V$, then $br\in M$, since an inverse $c\in V$ of $br$ would make $bc$ an inverse of $r$. In particular $0\in M$, $1\notin M$, and $-r\in M$ whenever $r\in M$.

proof.text: For nonzero $r,s\in E$, the hypothesis applied to $r/s$ says $r/s\in V$ or $s/r\in V$. Consequently, if $r,s\in M$ are nonzero and $r/s\in V$, then $r+s=s(1+r/s)\in M$ by Step 1; if $s/r\in V$, use $r+s=r(1+s/r)$. The zero cases are immediate. Thus $M$ is closed under addition, and every finite sum of elements of $M$ belongs to $M$. This is a direct calculation, without invoking a local-ring or maximal-ideal theorem.

proof.text: Fix $x\in E^\times$. By [def-weil-algebraic-element] there is a nonzero polynomial $P(T)=\sum_{i\in I}c_iT^i\in K[T]$ with $P(x)=0$, where $I$ is its finite nonempty set of exponents with nonzero coefficients. Put $d_i=c_ix^i\in E^\times$. Then $\sum_{i\in I}d_i=0$. There are at least two indices: a single term is nonzero because both its coefficient and $x$ are nonzero in a field.

proof.text: Choose $j\in I$ such that $d_i/d_j\in V$ for all $i\in I$. Here is the finite selection argument: start with any term, and process the remaining terms one at a time. If the new term divided by the current chosen term is in $V$, keep the choice. Otherwise their inverse ratio is in $V$, so replace the chosen term by the new one; every earlier term divided by the new choice is the product of its old ratio and the old choice divided by the new one, hence is in $V$. This induction ends because $I$ is finite.

proof.text: If $i>j$, the equation $t_i=(c_i/c_j)x^{i-j}$ gives $x^{i-j}=(c_j/c_i)t_i$; take $n=i-j$, $a=c_j/c_i\in K^\times$, and $u=t_i$. If $i<j$, invert the same equation to obtain $t_i^{-1}=(c_j/c_i)x^{j-i}$, hence $x^{j-i}=(c_i/c_j)t_i^{-1}$; take $n=j-i$, $a=c_i/c_j\in K^\times$, and $u=t_i^{-1}$. In both cases $n\ge1$ and $u,u^{-1}\in V$, as required.

proof.text: The set $U=V^\times$ is a subgroup of $E^\times$: products and inverses remain in $V$ together with their inverses. In the quotient group $E^\times/U$, the equality $x^n=au$ gives $[x]^n=[a]$ because $[u]=1$. Thus the positive multiple $n[x]$ lies in the image of $K^\times$, exactly the final clause.
